paragraphs.text: By birth Reuben is considered the firstborn, but he committed a great sin, which was his adultery with his father's wife, that is, his concubine or maidservant whom he had taken as a wife. Therefore the birthright, with its honor and its blessing, was taken from him and given to Joseph because of his godliness from his youth, then his love for his brothers, his forbearance with them, his forgiveness of them, his hosting them in Egypt and his care for them. So God gave him a double portion beyond his brothers, in that his two sons Ephraim and Manasseh each received the portion of a tribe in the land, that is, double, and not the portion of one tribe only. God wishes to declare here that the blessing is given to the one who fears Him and is taken from the one who makes light of His word.

Hold fast to God's commandments, that you may enjoy His care, His love and His blessings in your life. Every struggle you undertake is very precious to God, even if it is a cup of cold water, and God wants to reward you, so show your love for Him.
Prevailed: was exalted.

Here he points to the standing of the tribe of Judah, because from its descendants came Christ, the Author of our salvation and our Redeemer. Judah, then, has his standing, but the blessing went to Joseph because of his godliness. Because of the honor and importance of the tribe of Judah, he mentioned its genealogy at the beginning of this book, so as to arrive at King David, from whom Christ comes (chs. 2-4).

entries.section: (2) The genealogies of the tribe of Reuben

paragraphs.text: Tilgath-pilneser: he is the same as Tiglath-pileser (2 Kgs 15:29), the Assyrian king who carried away the kingdom of Israel into captivity.

Here he mentions the genealogies of the tribe of Reuben, beginning with Reuben and continuing to the Assyrian captivity in 722 BC. The tribe of Reuben was carried into captivity before the other tribes because it dwelt east of the Jordan River, that is, facing Assyria, which lay to the east of the land of the Jews. The span of time between the life of Reuben and the Assyrian captivity is about 1100 years, and it is therefore understood that the writer of this book did not mention all the genealogies of Reuben but abridged them, because of their lack of importance.
Hezron and Carmi, sons of Reuben, are not the ones mentioned in (ch. 2) among the descendants of Judah.

entries.section: (2) The genealogies of the tribe of Reuben

paragraphs.text: He continues the account of the descendants of Reuben, and mentions that they dwelt from Aroer to the region of Nebo, which is one of the peaks of the Jearim mountain range, and to the city of Baal-meon. All of these were cities and places that the tribe of Reuben possessed, east of the Jordan River and east of the Dead Sea. Moses went up Mount Nebo to see the land of Canaan, which God had promised to His people, before he died.
The registration by genealogy mentioned here means the one that took place in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel.

entries.section: (2) The genealogies of the tribe of Reuben

paragraphs.text: The tribe of Reuben was concerned to possess the fertile lands east of the Jordan River, even as far as the Euphrates River, which is in present-day Iraq. These regions are fertile pastures suitable for the livestock of the tribe of Reuben, and thus God's promise that the children of Israel would possess the land from the Euphrates to the river of Egypt is fulfilled. Reuben was not concerned to drive out the wicked in the regions neighboring him, but was concerned for the fertile land, which in time made him negligent and caused him to mingle with the wicked around him and to worship their gods. In choosing the fertile places and neglecting spiritual things he is like Lot, and he lost much, for he was the first of the tribes to be carried into captivity. He was not like Abraham, the father of the fathers, who obeyed God and lived in the wilderness, nor like Caleb the son of Jephunneh, who was concerned to possess the city of Hebron in the land of Canaan.

Be concerned for your spiritual goal, which is life with Christ and your place in the Kingdom, before your material ambitions, because the love of possessions hinders you and occupies your heart away from the love of God.

entries.section: (2) The genealogies of the tribe of Reuben

paragraphs.text: The Hagarites: probably the descendants of Hagar, that is, the descendants of Ishmael.
Gilead: the region lying east of the Jordan River. Its western part is fertile, while its eastern part is desert, and most of the land of Gilead lies in the portion of the tribe of Gad.

The book tells us that the descendants of Reuben waged war against the Hagarites in order to take their places, and they prevailed over them and took possession of their tents. This was in the days of Saul, the first of the kings of the children of Israel.

entries.section: (3) The genealogies of the tribe of Gad

paragraphs.text: Bashan: a fertile region lying northeast of the Jordan River, reaching northward to the sources of the river, and famous for its oak trees.
Salchah: a fertile region lying east of Bashan.
The descendants of Gad dwelt north of the descendants of Reuben and settled in the region of Bashan, as far as Salchah, which was within the eastern borders of the kingdom of the children of Israel.

entries.section: (3) The genealogies of the tribe of Gad

paragraphs.text: Sharon: a fertile region lying east of the Jordan River, which is different from the Sharon that lies west of the Jordan River toward the Mediterranean Sea.

Here he mentions some of the descendants of Gad, those who lived in the days of the Assyrian captivity, in order to make clear that it was because of their sins that they went into captivity (2 Kgs 15:29).

entries.section: (3) The genealogies of the tribe of Gad

paragraphs.text: This shows the concern of the descendants of Gad to record their names in the genealogy, which was made in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam II king of Israel.

It is good for you to know your lineage, that you are a Christian, a son of the King of kings and Lord of lords, so that you do not become lax toward evil desires, but learn that you are the head of all creation, to lead it in praising and thanking God. Do not be distracted from your prayer, so that you may always live in purity.

Here he tells us in detail of the war that took place between the children of Israel and the Hagarites. The people of God who dwelt east of the Jordan River gathered, namely the men of the tribes of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh. Their number was great, 44,760, and they were men trained for war with swords, shields, bows and all the instruments of war.
The people of God set out to fight a group of tribes, all of them descendants of Ishmael, who dwelt in Gilead, in its eastern region.
The book makes clear the secret of the victory of the people of God over the Hagarites, which was their prayer and their trust in God; by the power of God they prevailed over them.

If you trust in God, be sure that you are able to overcome all the armies of the demons, because they are nothing before His power, however great your weakness. Do not be troubled by the multitude of your falls, but be strong in faith and seek God in humility, confident that by His power you are able to triumph over all your sins.
God's blessing is shown in the abundance of spoil that His people gained from their war with the Hagarites, and likewise in the vast numbers of captives.

It is evident from this verse that the war was severe, and the people of God killed a great number of the descendants of Ishmael. The victory depended on God's presence with His people; although they were trained for war and their number was great, their reliance was on God. They took possession of their lands and dwelt in them, but sadly they did not continue in purity of heart and in their worship of God, so God allowed them to be carried into captivity, that they might repent and return to Him once again.
The book tells us about the descendants of Levi in order to arrive at the priests, whose head is Aaron, the grandson of Kohath the son of Levi.

Amram begot three children: Moses, Aaron and Miriam. Moses is the leader and chief who delivered his people, Aaron is the high priest, and Miriam is the prophetess. Thus Levi begot deliverance, the priesthood and prophecy, and all of these are united in Christ, for they are types of Him.
Aaron begot four sons, two of whom, Nadab and Abihu, died without offspring because they offered strange fire, and so they represent the punishment of disobedience.

Eleazar is the priest whom the grace of God chose, and from his descendants came Jehozadak, who went into captivity, and then his grandson Jeshua, who returned from the captivity and served as priest in the house that he built with Zerubbabel (Hag 1:1). After that the priestly lineage became obscure for more than 300 years, until Christ the Great High Priest was born.

As for Ithamar, his descendants were excluded from the priesthood because of their evils. Among them were Eli the priest and his son Phinehas, and the last of them was Abiathar, whom King Solomon removed.

The book mentions the descendants of Aaron until it reaches Ahitub, who was a priest in the days of Saul, the first of the kings of the children of Israel. It is noted that it does not mention all the descendants, because the time between Levi and the return from the captivity is about 1300 years, so that it includes far more than the names written in this genealogy; it has omitted many because of their lack of importance.
In this sequence it mentions Zadok, who was high priest in the days of David, and his son Ahimaaz, who gave warning of the conspiracy of Absalom and saved David from death.
The Johanan mentioned here is probably Jehoiada, who preserved King Joash and raised him, until he anointed him king at the age of seven over the kingdom of Judah (2 Kgs 11:4).

This Azariah is probably the high priest who tried to prevent King Uzziah from entering the house of the Lord to burn incense; and since the king refused, God struck him with leprosy because of his presumption against the priesthood and his disobedience to Azariah the high priest (2 Chr 26:17-20). Here the godly high priests appear: Jehoiada protects the blessed offspring Joash from the evil of Queen Athaliah, and Azariah shows his holy zeal for the house of God, as he tries to prevent the king from presuming against the priesthood.

Be faithful in carrying out your responsibilities, whatever dangers you may meet, because God is with you, protecting you, guiding you and supporting you, as He was with the godly men in every generation.
Here in the genealogies of Aaron we see names repeated for other persons, such as the repetition of the names Ahitub and Zadok, who are different from those who lived in the days of Saul and David.

At the end of this sequence we see Jehozadak the high priest, who lived in the days of the Babylonian captivity and went away with the captives. As for his father Seraiah the high priest, Nebuchadnezzar killed him at the attack on Jerusalem. We notice that Eleazar the high priest, the son of Aaron, came out of the bondage of Egypt and was established as a priest in the wilderness of Sinai, while Jehozadak his descendant went out from Jerusalem into the bondage of captivity, and this was because of the negligence and evil of the people of God and its priests. God saves His children from afflictions, but because of their sins they need His discipline once again.

entries.section: (5) The mighty men from all the tribes at Hebron to make David king

paragraphs.text: This part, mentioned here from (vv. 1-5), was referred to by the Second Book of Samuel in (2 Sam 6:

1), that is, it mentioned it briefly, whereas here he explains to us the details of the event, which is that after David became king over all Israel, he thought before everything else of bringing the ark of the covenant of the Lord to Jerusalem, so that his throne might be beside the ark. The gathering of the people around God, represented in the ark of His covenant, came before their gathering around the king, and this shows David's humility, his faith and his submission to God.

So he gathered the commanders of his army and the heads of the tribes, that is, all those in authority in Israel, and consulted them about moving the ark of the covenant of God from the city of Jearim to Jerusalem. He did this so that the tribes would not be displeased at the presence of the ark within the kingdom of Judah beside the king, but that it might be with their counsel and agreement, and this shows David's wisdom and his concern to please all the tribes.

The people of God had been divided into thousands and hundreds since the days of Moses (Num 31:14, Deut 1:15), to make it easy to lead them and to convey news to them. So David gathered the captains of thousands and captains of hundreds, because they represent the whole people, in order to take with them a political and administrative decision, which was the moving of the ark, and he summoned the priests, as we shall see in the following verses, because it was at the same time a religious act.

entries.section: (5) The mighty men from all the tribes at Hebron to make David king

paragraphs.text: Their suburbs: the areas surrounding the cities of the Levites, used for pasturing sheep, extending two thousand cubits around the city in which they dwell.

David spoke with the heads of the tribes of Israel, who represent all the people of God, and he spoke to them concerning bringing up the ark of the covenant of God and moving it from the place where it was, the city of Jearim, to Jerusalem, where David reigns. In this he wished to gather all the peoples around God, represented in the ark of His covenant, and not around himself as their king. And he said two things to them:
1- "If it seem good unto you," that is, if you agree to this. This shows his kindness, his humility and his concern to please his people.

2- "And that it be of the Lord our God," that is, David's concern for the mind of God, before whom he prays that he may hear His voice; only then would he move the ark. The mind of God was more important to David than anything else; therefore he prayed first, before speaking to the heads of Israel.
David asked the leaders to send word to all the people in their places, that they might come and bring up the ark of the covenant of God. He says "bring up" because Jerusalem is built on five hills.
David stressed the summoning of the priests and the Levites, because they are the servants of God who would carry the ark and minister to it.

We notice David's love and humility in calling the people his brethren, and he did not exalt himself over them as a king. He is a type of Christ, who calls those who believe in Him His brethren (Heb 2:11). We also see that the priests and the Levites had been scattered throughout all the land of Israel, because the service of the ark had ceased since the days of Eli the priest, when the Philistines took the ark and then sent it back, and it remained for a time in the city of Jearim.

entries.section: (5) The mighty men from all the tribes at Hebron to make David king

paragraphs.text: David felt the sin of the people of God, that they had forgotten the ark of the covenant of God throughout the days of Saul's reign, because of Saul's distance from God. But David's humility and sense of responsibility made him ascribe the fault to himself and to all the people, so that he said "we enquired not." Humility made David ascribe the fault to himself and not condemn others.

May you turn the blame upon yourself when mistakes occur in which you shared with others, and not incline to condemnation, because your repentance and humility bring upon you the mercies of God, while your condemnation brings upon you the wrath of God and His judgment.

David said, "let us bring again the ark of our God," because the ark had been set down at the beginning of the entrance of the people of God into the Promised Land, at Gilgal (Josh 5:10), for a short time in the days of Joshua, and then was moved to Shiloh (1 Sam 1:3) and remained there about three hundred years, until the days of Samuel. After that the Philistines took it (1 Sam 5), when they triumphed over the children of Israel, and they were struck with many diseases, so they sent the ark to Beth-shemesh (1 Sam 6:12), a Jewish city, but the people were not careful in approaching the ark, and fifty thousand of them died, so they moved it to the city of Jearim (1 Sam 7:1), and it remained there throughout the reign of Saul. The ark alone was moved to these places, from the Philistines to Beth Shemesh to Jearim, while the remaining parts of the tabernacle of meeting were moved from Shiloh to the city of Nob and remained there throughout the days of Saul. The separation of the ark from the tabernacle was temporary, from the time the Philistines took it until it returned again in the days of Solomon, when he placed it in the Temple.

entries.section: (5) The mighty men from all the tribes at Hebron to make David king

paragraphs.text: The leaders obeyed David's word and informed the people in their cities of the intention to bring up the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and the people agreed, and even showed their concern for this matter. The leaders informed David of the readiness of all to carry out what he had proposed. This shows the love of the leaders and the people for God, and so they agreed and obeyed their king readily.

entries.section: (5) The mighty men from all the tribes at Hebron to make David king

paragraphs.text: Shihor: a word meaning black, and it is meant to refer to the Nile of Egypt, which carries silt; probably there was a branch of the Nile extending into the desert of Sinai, and this is what is meant by Shihor.
Hamath: a city lying north of Damascus, at a distance of 190 km north of Damascus.
Jearim: a village lying on the border between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, north of Jerusalem, at a distance of 14 km.

David gathered the people of the children of Israel from the farthest reaches of their land, that is, beside the desert of Sinai and the river Shihor, to the farthest north, that is, beside Hamath, and they all moved to the city of Jearim to bring the ark of the covenant of God from it to Jerusalem.
(2) The death of Uzza (vv. 6-11:)

6- And David went up, and all Israel, to Baalah, that is, to Kirjathjearim, which belonged to Judah, to bring up thence the ark of God the Lord, that dwelleth between the cherubims, whose name is called on it. 7- And they carried the ark of God in a new cart out of the house of Abinadab: and Uzza and Ahio drave the cart. 8- And David and all Israel played before God with all their might, and with singing, and with harps, and with psalteries, and with timbrels, and with cymbals, and with trumpets. 9- And when they came unto the threshingfloor of Chidon, Uzza put forth his hand to hold the ark; for the oxen stumbled. 10- And the anger of the Lord was kindled against Uzza, and he smote him, because he put forth his hand to the ark: and there he died before God. 11- And David was displeased, because the Lord had made a breach upon Uzza: wherefore that place is called Perezuzza to this day.

These events were recorded in the text in (2 Sam 6:2-8) and were explained in the book al-Mawsu'a (the Encyclopedia), Part Five. In summary, David erred in that he placed the ark on two oxen, contrary to the Law, which requires that only the priests carry it. Despite his joy and the joy of all the people and his proud dancing to the sound of the music, God declared His anger through the rushing of the oxen, until the ark was in danger of falling to the ground. Then Uzza the son of Abinadab, who served the ark in his father's house, rushed forward and stretched out his hand and touched the ark, and fell dead at once, because no man is permitted to touch the ark. So David grieved over the death of Uzza, and he forgot his own error in imitating the Philistines, who placed the ark on a new cart drawn by two cows. But the Philistines had their excuse, since they were pagans who did not know the Law of God, whereas David knew the Law and how the ark was to be carried, as God had commanded.

It also reminds us that before the ark His name was called upon, that is, the people of God worshiped Him and called upon His name and did not mention strange gods, because the ark represents the presence of God.

David rejoiced at bringing back the ark, but he did not obey the Law of God concerning how to move the ark, and so God was angry. May you, when you pray and praise and do works of goodness to rejoice the heart of God, be concerned to obey His commandments and all that the Church teaches, that you may pray and serve in the way God wants, and not imitate the people of the world, for you are different from them; for when David imitated the Philistines in moving the ark, God was angry.
(3) The blessing of the house of Obed-edom (vv. 12-14:)

12- And David was afraid of God that day, saying, How shall I bring the ark of God home to me? 13- So David brought not the ark home to himself to the city of David, but carried it aside into the house of Obededom the Gittite. 14- And the ark of God remained with the family of Obededom in his house three months. And the Lord blessed the house of Obededom, and all that he had. These verses were explained previously in (2 Sam 6:9-11), and in summary what happened was David's fear of God when He struck Uzza, so he placed the ark in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite for three months and did not move it to Jerusalem.

When you fear God, this calls you to keep away from sin and not from God, because He makes you afraid so that you may keep away from evil, but He has compassion on you with His care and His fatherhood and satisfies you. So when you sin, do not withdraw from Him in shame, but stand before Him in prayer and prostrate yourself in His presence, offering repentance, and you will obtain His mercies and forgiveness.
The First Book of Kings: King David became great

These verses were explained in (2 Sam 5:11, 12), and in them we see how God established David's kingdom: Hiram king of Tyre, which was one of the great cities at that time, sent to bless him on his reign, and he presented him with many gifts.
If you please God with your love, your repentance and your good works, God will bless you and give you favor in the eyes of those around you, that you may grow in love for Him and in the love of all.
(2) The sons of David in Jerusalem (vv. 3 - 7:)-

3- And David took more wives at Jerusalem: and David begat more sons and daughters. 4- Now these are the names of his children which he had in Jerusalem; Shammua, and Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon, 5- And Ibhar, and Elishua, and Elpalet, 6- And Nogah, and Nepheg, and Japhia, 7- And Elishama, and Beeliada, and Eliphalet.

We explained these verses in (2 Sam 5:13-16), and in them we see God's blessing on David in the many sons and daughters born to him in Jerusalem. He is a type of Christ, who has many sons and daughters who have believed in Him in the whole world.

Be careful to adorn yourself with the virtues, which are counted as sons and daughters to you, so that through them you may sense God in your life and by them be made worthy to enter the Kingdom of Heaven. The closer you cling to God, the more virtues He bestows on you.

These events were mentioned briefly in (2 Sam 6:12, 13). What happened was that David understood his error in the way he moved the ark and his violation of the Law, since the priests did not carry it but they placed it on a cart. Therefore the oxen rushed forward and Uzza died, and he offered repentance to God, especially after he saw God's blessing on the house of Obed-edom because of the presence of the ark with him.

So David prepared a tent in Jerusalem, after he had built houses for himself and for the administration of the kingdom, and this tent was to receive the ark. As for the tabernacle of meeting, with its remaining parts, it was in the city of Gibeon. Abiathar, the second high priest, was in Jerusalem to serve the ark, and this arrangement was temporary and ended in the days of Solomon, after the building of the Temple, when Zadok alone became the high priest for the service of the Temple in Jerusalem. David gathered all the people of Israel who were concerned for the worship of God in Jerusalem and declared to them what the Law prescribes, which is that the ark of the covenant of God may be carried by no one but the priests only. This shows David's humility, since he declared his error of the first time before all the people, so that everyone would be bound by the Law of God.

Be strong enough to apologize for your error, and do not justify yourself or try to cover the sin, because God rejoices in His repentant children, and people also will respect you for your frankness and humility, and by this, without knowing it, you teach them true humility.

David gathered a great number of priests and Levites, eight hundred and sixty-two, under the leadership of six chiefs, to carry out the service of the ark. This shows his concern to involve everyone in the service so that they might receive its blessing, and his great concern for the service of God, so that he gathered for Him all this huge number.

After David gathered the high priests Zadok and Abiathar and all the chiefs, the priests and the Levites, he declared to them that their sin in not carrying the ark, and being content to place it on a cart, was the reason for God's anger. He also declared to them the necessity of preparing themselves by purifying themselves to carry out this great service, which was the moving of the ark of the covenant of God. Then he added the necessity of their commitment that the priests carry the ark with poles, as the Law prescribes, that is, as God decreed. The rest of the Levites were to help them. So everyone obeyed and purified themselves and carried the ark from the house of Obed-edom.
The Second Book of Samuel tells us how greatly David honored the ark, in the sacrifices he offered before the ark throughout its journey from the house of Obed-edom to Jerusalem.
(2) The singers before the ark (vv. 16 - 24:)-

16- And David spake to the chief of the Levites to appoint their brethren to be the singers with instruments of musick, psalteries and harps and cymbals, sounding, by lifting up the voice with joy. 17- So the Levites appointed Heman the son of Joel; and of his brethren, Asaph the son of Berechiah; and of the sons of Merari their brethren, Ethan the son of Kushaiah; 18- And with them their brethren of the second degree, Zechariah, Ben, and Jaaziel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehiel, and Unni, Eliab, and Benaiah, and Maaseiah, and Mattithiah, and Elipheleh, and Mikneiah, and Obededom, and Jeiel, the porters.

19- So the singers, Heman, Asaph, and Ethan, were appointed to sound with cymbals of brass; 20- And Zechariah, and Aziel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehiel, and Unni, and Eliab, and Maaseiah, and Benaiah, with psalteries on Alamoth; 21- And Mattithiah, and Elipheleh, and Mikneiah, and Obededom, and Jeiel, and Azaziah, with harps on the Sheminith to excel. 22- And Chenaniah, chief of the Levites, was for song: he instructed about the song, because he was skilful. 23- And Berechiah and Elkanah were doorkeepers for the ark. 24- And Shebaniah, and Jehoshaphat, and Nethaneel, and Amasai, and Zechariah, and Benaiah, and Eliezer, the priests, did blow with the trumpets before the ark of God: and Obededom and Jehiah were doorkeepers for the ark.
Harps: plural of the lute ('ud), an ancient musical instrument, which still exists to this day. It is a box with strings on it.
Psalteries: a small ancient stringed instrument, over which usually a single string is stretched.
Cymbals: plural of cymbal, and they are the cymbals used in our churches now. They are made of brass, and when they touch they produce sounds that regulate and lead the hymns and praises.

David was also concerned to present spiritual songs before the ark, in honor of God. So David asked the chiefs of the Levites to gather the singers and give them musical instruments, such as harps, psalteries and cymbals, so that the songs would be accompanied by suitable music.
David chose three of the singers, distinguished in leadership, namely Asaph, with Heman and Ethan, and made them chiefs over the singers.
Of the second degree: the assistants, that is, those who are in the second rank after the leaders.
He also chose fourteen men of the singers, distinguished ones, to be assistants to the three chiefs of the singers mentioned above.
We notice that these assistants in leading the singers were at the same time doorkeepers, that is, responsible for guarding the ark.
19-21: Leading the singers. David divided the work in organizing the singing, and David gave these responsibilities:-

1- The leadership, as we mentioned, was given to Asaph, Heman and Ethan, to lead the singers by means of the cymbals, just as happens now, when the head deacon leads the rest of the deacons and the people, using the cymbals.

2- He assigned six of the singers to use the psalteries, to present a high register of the voice, called the "jawab" (the upper register), which in the Jesuit translation is "the melody of the maidens," and which corresponds now to the range called "Tenor."

3- He also chose six of the singers to sing in a low register called the "qarar" (the lower register), so these six lead this voice, which corresponds now to the Basses, and they lead it with the harps.
- David chose a chief from the Levites whose responsibility was the carrying, or the moving, that is, he was responsible for carrying the ark and moving it.
- David also chose from the Levites two groups, each of which carried out a particular responsibility, namely:-
1- The doorkeepers of the ark, that is, those responsible for guarding it while it was being moved, or after it was placed in the tent. He assigned four persons here to carry out this responsibility.

2- David chose seven of the priests for the responsibility of blowing the trumpets before the ark. The trumpet is a musical instrument with a loud sound, made of bronze or silver, and it gives honor and majesty to the ark and alerts the people to stand, or to bow down, and to honor the ark.

How great David was in his concern for the ark and his honoring of it! And you, are you concerned to honor God in the Church, by coming early and concentrating in the prayers, so that you may enjoy the sense of Him and rejoice in Him?
(3) David's dancing before the ark (vv. 25 - 29:)-

25- So David, and the elders of Israel, and the captains over thousands, went to bring up the ark of the covenant of the Lord out of the house of Obededom with joy. 26- And it came to pass, when God helped the Levites that bare the ark of the covenant of the Lord, that they offered seven bullocks and seven rams. 27- And David was clothed with a robe of fine linen, and all the Levites that bare the ark, and the singers, and Chenaniah the master of the song with the singers: David also had upon him an ephod of linen. 28- Thus all Israel brought up the ark of the covenant of the Lord with shouting, and with sound of the cornet, and with trumpets, and with cymbals, making a noise with psalteries and harps.

29- And it came to pass, as the ark of the covenant of the Lord came to the city of David, that Michal the daughter of Saul looking out at a window saw king David dancing and playing: and she despised him in her heart. This subject was mentioned with other details in (2 Sam 6:12 - 16)

Here he specifies those who went to bring up the ark from the house of Obed-edom, namely King David, the elders of the people and the captains of thousands, that is, all the leaders of the people. Of course a great number of the people followed them, and they were filled with joy, since the blessing of the Lord had been shown to the house of Obed-edom when the ark was with him for three months (ch. 13:14).

When you see God's blessing on His saints and His children in every generation, follow their example, walk with God as they did, and strive in the way of their virtues, and you also will receive a blessing from God, and by this, without feeling it, you will become a light to the world and draw many to God.

- The fear of God was upon the hearts of the priests and the Levites, who were charged with carrying the ark of the covenant and walking behind it, because of the death of Uzza. Therefore the grace of God intervened to help them and reassure them as they carried the ark. Here we find joy mingled with fear, which made them offer seven bullocks and seven rams, in addition to sacrificing an ox and a fatling whenever the priests who bore the ark had gone six paces (2 Sam 6:13).

(David took off his great royal garments and put on, like the priests, garments of linen. This was humility on David's part, and at the same time it represented his sanctification of the ark. The clothes that David wore were an ephod and a robe, which are two garments, one of which reaches to the feet and the other is shorter than it. The high priest used to wear them, and in special cases other persons wore them, such as Samuel (1 Sam 2:18). David here is a type of Christ the King, Priest and Prophet, since each of them wore linen.
Cornets: plural of sur, a trumpet made from the horn of an animal.

The people walked with the priests who bore the ark, the king, the elders and the chiefs, and they shouted with great joy, and they used various musical instruments, such as psalteries and harps and loud-sounding instruments such as trumpets.

The procession of the ark reached the city of David, which is a part of Jerusalem, and everyone was shouting with joy, and with them the king, who was dancing before the ark with all his might, because he was in great joy. When his wife Michal, the daughter of Saul, looked out from the window of her house, she saw David dancing, wearing linen garments, having taken off his royal clothes, and she despised him. This shows her weak esteem for the greatness of God and the holiness of the ark; therefore David rebuked her afterward.
David's praise and the service of the ark

entries.section: (1) The burnt offerings and the praise before the ark

paragraphs.text: These verses were mentioned in (2 Sam 6:17-19). A question may arise: why did David not bring the tabernacle and what was in it from Gibeon to Jerusalem to place the ark in it, but set up a special tent in Jerusalem in which he placed the ark? The reason, as we think, is that David intended to establish a permanent temple for God in Jerusalem in which to place the ark, but God told him that his son was the one who would build the Temple and not he. The tabernacle had been at Shiloh, as we mentioned, and in it the ark (ch. 13:3); then after the Philistines took the ark, the tabernacle was moved to Nob (1 Sam 21:1-9), and after Saul killed the priests at Nob (1 Sam 22:17-19) the tabernacle was moved to Gibeon (ch. 16:39, ch. 21:29). Thus David finally achieved what his heart longed for and declared in Psalm (132:3, 4), that his heart would not rest, nor settle in his house, nor would he give sleep to his eyes, until he found a place for the Lord. This was fulfilled when he placed the ark of the covenant in a tent in Jerusalem, to offer to Him holy service and worship.

entries.section: (1) The burnt offerings and the praise before the ark

paragraphs.text: To record: to remember God's benefits and thank Him for them.

Here the book adds David's arrangement of the service of praise before the ark of the covenant of God, and shows that the leader of the singers was Asaph, and with him a great number of Levites and also the priests, and they had the musical instruments, to glorify God in groups and in a fixed order. David had prepared a song for this occasion, which he gave to Asaph and the singers to repeat with music before the ark, and we shall explain this song in the following verses.

Asaph wrote twelve psalms within the Book of Psalms, and he took care to teach his sons praise, so that one hundred and twenty-eight of his descendants returned from the captivity trained in praise (Ezra 2:41), and they praised at the renewal of the Temple in the days of Ezra the priest (Ezra 3:10). Thus David offered two things to the ark of God:
1- Peace offerings and thanksgiving.
2- Praise.

It is noted that the number of chiefs of the singers mentioned in (vv. 5, 6) is smaller than those mentioned in (ch. 15), because some of the singers were before the ark in Jerusalem under the leadership of Asaph, and another group of the singers were under the leadership of Heman and Jeduthun before the tabernacle in Gibeon (vv. 41, 42).

If you love God, you will spontaneously wish to praise Him, to rejoice His heart and rejoice with Him. So be careful to take part in the Midnight Praise (Tasbeha) in the Church, that you may become accustomed to it and love it and enjoy it also in your private room.

David calls the people to thank God and to mention His name and His benefits, so that it may spread among the nations and they may believe in God. That is, he asks three things of the people: thanksgiving, prayer and preaching, as he says (give thanks, call upon, make known).

David asks the people to be concerned for praise, in saying "sing" and "sing psalms," and also that the conversations of the people with one another be filled with talk about the wondrous works of God with them, so that they may live a life of thanksgiving.
David shows the blessings of praise, since it gives the one who praises:
1- Boasting and confidence in the soul that trusts in God.
2- Joy and consolation that cannot be expressed.

When a person discovers, through praise, the greatness of God, he seeks His help and His strength (His might), and even seeks Him continually, so that he comes to trust in Him at all times and enters into what is called the life of prayer.

It shows the importance of repeating the works of God (His marvellous works) and thanking Him for them, in addition to His commandments and His Law (the judgments of His mouth), for repeating the word of God establishes it in the heart and influences a person's conduct, so that he lives for God.

He rejoices the hearts of the people of God, who are the descendants of Jacob Israel, with the truth that God is our God, that is, we are His own and His chosen, and this gives them reassurance and strength, because He is the Ruler of all (His judgments are in all the earth).

David directs them to remember the promises of God that He gave to their fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, which are promises of blessing for their descendants if they keep His commandments, that is, David warns them to keep the commandments of God so that they may enjoy His covenants.

By "a thousand generations" he means the continuation of God's covenants forever. Heaven and earth will pass away, but the word of God will not pass away, and the steadfastness of God's promises calls us to praise Him continually.

The cord of your inheritance: lands were measured with ropes of a certain length, and what is meant here is the land of Canaan, which God gave as an inheritance to His people; He measured it and knew its area and granted it to them. David reminds his people of the fulfillment of God's promises, which were fulfilled in them, for they were few in number in the days of Jacob, to whom God promised the inheritance of the land of Canaan. This was indeed fulfilled, when God brought His people out of Egypt and they crossed the wilderness of Sinai, then entered and possessed the land of Canaan after hundreds of years. They were seventy men in the days of Jacob, and they entered the land of Canaan numbering approximately two million.

Trust in God's promises to you, however weak you may seem and however limited your resources, for He is able to bless you and to work miracles in you, and after this do not forget to thank Him always.

The people of God, a small number, represented in the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, moved from nation to nation, namely Egypt and Gerar, and God kept them while they were in these kingdoms, so that no one could wrong them. Indeed God rebuked Pharaoh of Egypt (Gen 12:17) when he took Sarah, and likewise Abimelech king of Gerar (Gen 20:3), whom God rebuked in a dream because he had taken Sarah to marry her. This was despite the weakness of the fathers before the power of these kings, but their mighty God kept them and defended them, so these kings sought the blessing of the fathers.

Here God declares His keeping of His children and His prevention of the world from hindering His children from their service. "The anointed ones" is the plural of "anointed" (messiah), meaning one anointed with oil, but the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were set apart for God, and they alone believed in Him in the midst of the world, so they were like the anointed. The fathers were not prophets, that is, they did not speak prophecies, but they proclaimed the voice of God by their lives in the world, as the prophets proclaim the voice of God by their prophecies.

Here begins the part taken from (Ps 96), in which he calls the whole world, and not only the people of God, to praise Him, and he demands that those who believe in God preach Him among all the nations, because Christ will come to die for the whole world.

He asks that the preaching be "from day to day," that is, that it continue in the Old Testament and the New Testament and throughout the generations, so that the nations may see God in those who believe in Him.

David demands of the believers that they proclaim God's benefits and His wondrous works in the universe, to alert all the nations and peoples, that they may return to God. And when the world sees the prayers and praises of the believers, how strong and fervent they are, they will believe in their great God, because of the sincerity of their feelings.

Why do the believers glorify God? Because God is different from all the pagan gods; He is greater than all gods, glorious (praised) and to be feared, that is, feared by all, because all authority is in His hand. The heavenly beings fear Him, and consequently the earthly beings must glorify Him and fear Him.

On the other hand, all the pagan gods are statues of idols that neither speak nor feel; rather, they are tools in the hand of Satan. But God is the true living One, who made the heavens and the earth and all that is in them.

In God is perfect purity and beauty, so His presence, that is, His place, rises above every thought in its greatness. Before Him shine His majesty and His blessing, which are shown in His angels and His saints who surround Him. And the strength of God, that is, His power, is in mercy and love for mankind; therefore it gladdens and delights the hearts of His children.
Give: bestow a gift, that is, offer a donation and a gift to God.

David calls all the nations to submit to God and offer Him gifts and offerings, in glorification of His greatness, and for their worship to be in purity and cleanness of heart, and this is the holy adornment. These offerings are considered praise and thanksgiving to God, the Creator of all and their Provider, who does good to all peoples (Heb 13:15, 16).

David calls all mankind to fear God, so that they may behave well and no one wrong another, and so live in stability and peace, and the whole world be established in tranquility, and the devil be unable to create disturbances and divisions, by his stirring up evil desires in hearts.

If people fear God, they can then share with the heavenly beings in seeing God and glorifying Him, and so they rejoice, and God reigns over their hearts as He reigns over the heavenly beings, and they come to true happiness.
Roar: the waves of the sea crash with force and make a terrifying sound.

The sea is a symbol of the world, which is always troubled and disturbed, but it does not affect the children of God, who are settled in His fear, because with God they are stronger than the world, and indeed He subjects the world to them. And the wilderness, which is the barren, deserted land, let it rejoice, because God populates it with solitary monks, who have lived in it from the days of Elijah in the Old Testament until today.
The wood: deserted places, in which wild trees grow that bear no fruit.

David continues his sense of the submission of all creatures and their joy in God, who reigns over them, and that His coming is near, to judge the evil that is in the world and remove it. The trees of the wood are a symbol of the Gentiles who were without fruit, but when they believe in Christ the Redeemer and submit to Him, they become His children and bear fruit and rejoice at His coming, to judge the evil in the world and raise them with Him to the Kingdom.
David ends this part of the song with the praise of God, because He is good; indeed He alone is perfectly good in this world, and He deserves praise and glorification forever.

David speaks, in the spirit of prophecy, about the people of God who will be scattered in captivity, and he asks God to save them and bring them back to their land to worship Him in His Temple, and to rescue them from the hands of the nations, that they may live praising and glorifying His great person, and this is their essential work.

David concludes his song, blessing God and calling all the people to join in prayer and glorification of Him, as He is blessed and glorified from eternity and to eternity. The people responded to David's call and said "Amen," declaring their agreement with all that Asaph and the singers with him had uttered, and indeed they all joined in the praise of God, that is, the whole people sang a hymn that they knew.

entries.section: (3) The guarding and service of the ark and the tabernacle

paragraphs.text: David's song, which the singers chanted under the leadership of Asaph, was the introduction to an order that David established for offering praises daily before the ark in Jerusalem. By this God's place was restored in His holy city, Jerusalem, and the hearts of the people returned to Him, that He might be their God in all their steps, and that they might glorify Him and seek Him in all their needs.

If David organized praises daily before God in the Old Testament, how much more ought praises to be offered today in the Church, at every time, so that we may share with the heavenly beings who praise continually.
May you taste the praise of God every day, even with a short hymn, that you may enjoy fellowship with Him, and your heart rejoice and rejoice His heart.

entries.section: (3) The guarding and service of the ark and the tabernacle

paragraphs.text: David also appointed doorkeepers to guard the ark. It is mentioned that their number was sixty-eight, and they were under the leadership of Obed-edom and his eight brothers, in addition to another person also called Obed-edom, and his companion Hosah. From this David's concern for the ark of the covenant of God appears, as he organized everything pertaining to its service.

entries.section: (3) The guarding and service of the ark and the tabernacle

paragraphs.text: Gibeon: a city lying northwest of Jerusalem at a distance of five miles.

On the other hand, David was concerned for the service of God before the tabernacle of meeting, which was in the city of Gibeon, with all its parts except the ark of the covenant of God, and the city of Gibeon was built on a high place. David arranged that Zadok the high priest and his brothers the priests should be responsible for the service at Gibeon, while Abiathar, the high priest, was responsible for the service in Jerusalem. This was a temporary arrangement in the days of David, that is, the existence of two high priests, but in the days of Solomon Zadok alone became high priest.

entries.section: (3) The guarding and service of the ark and the tabernacle

paragraphs.text: Zadok and all the priests were concerned to fulfill the Law and to offer the morning and evening burnt offering every day, to declare their love for God and their attachment to Him.

Be concerned to pray every day, morning and evening, so that you begin your day and end it with God. Force yourself at the beginning, so that you become accustomed to prayer, and then you will move to the stage of delight and enjoyment of God, and your sense of His presence with you, and His blessings in your life, as you become a son who is near to Him. Open your heart and speak to Him as a son. Thank Him for His benefits and confess your sins before Him, then ask of Him what you want for yourself and for others.

entries.section: (3) The guarding and service of the ark and the tabernacle

paragraphs.text: Here we find David's concern to arrange the service of praise before the tabernacle of meeting also, so the singers under the leadership of Heman and Jeduthun stand for continual praise, as Asaph leads the praise before the ark of the covenant in Jerusalem, because David felt that the mercies of the Lord are upon His people forever, and so He ought to be thanked at all times for this.
The singers used musical instruments with the praises; these instruments were trumpets, cymbals and various other instruments.
David was also concerned to guard the tabernacle, so he appointed doorkeepers under the leadership of Jeduthun.

entries.section: (3) The guarding and service of the ark and the tabernacle

paragraphs.text: After the celebration of placing the ark in Jerusalem was over, and the service for it was arranged, as well as the service of the tabernacle at Gibeon, the people departed, each to his house, and David also, to complete the prayer and the praise of God in their houses. This shows the importance of family prayer in the home, for it is the natural extension of the congregational prayer with the rest of the people in the Church, because a person's love for God in the Church must be accompanied by prayer at home, and family prayer confirms the family's bond and its unity in the love of God. This book did not mention the sin of Michal, David's wife, and her contempt for him when he danced before the ark (2 Sam 6:16), because the book here concentrates on David's love for God and how he is a type of Christ.
God's view on the building of His house
A'nash: one who has six fingers on the foot or the hand.

This chapter was mentioned previously in (2 Sam 11:1, 12:26-31, 21:18-22). In it we find David's victory over the capital of the children of Ammon, the city of Rabbah, and his capture of it. Likewise his victory over the giants of the Philistines at Gezer and Gath.

People may boast of their strength, their wealth and their positions, or because of some capability they have, but all this is passing away. May you stand firm in your faith, knowing that the threats of the wicked are temporary and will come to an end, and that God allows them to test your faith and your humility.
David's census of the people

1- And Satan stood up against Israel, and provoked David to number Israel. 2- And David said to Joab and to the rulers of the people, Go, number Israel from Beersheba even to Dan; and bring the number of them to me, that I may know it. 3- And Joab answered, The Lord make his people an hundred times so many more as they be: but, my lord the king, are they not all my lord's servants? why then doth my lord require this thing? why will he be a cause of trespass to Israel? 4- Nevertheless the king's word prevailed against Joab. Wherefore Joab departed, and went throughout all Israel, and came to Jerusalem. 5- And Joab gave the sum of the number of the people unto David. And all they of Israel were a thousand thousand and an hundred thousand men that drew sword: and Judah was four hundred threescore and ten thousand men that drew sword. 6- But Levi and Benjamin counted he not among them: for the king's word was abominable to Joab. 7- And God was displeased with this thing; therefore he smote Israel. 8- And David said unto God, I have sinned greatly, because I have done this thing: but now, I beseech thee, do away the iniquity of thy servant; for I have done very foolishly. 9- And the Lord spake unto Gad, David's seer, saying, 10- Go and tell David, saying, Thus saith the Lord, I offer thee three things: choose thee one of them, that I may do it unto thee. 11- So Gad came to David, and said unto him, Thus saith the Lord, Choose thee 12- Either three years' famine; or three months to be destroyed before thy foes, while that the sword of thine enemies overtaketh thee; or else three days the sword of the Lord, even the pestilence, in the land, and the angel of the Lord destroying throughout all the coasts of Israel. Now therefore advise thyself what word I shall bring again to him that sent me. 13- And David said unto Gad, I am in a great strait: let me fall now into the hand of the Lord; for very great are his mercies: but let me not fall into the hand of man. 14- So the Lord sent pestilence upon Israel: and there fell of Israel seventy thousand men. 15- And God sent an angel unto Jerusalem to destroy it: and as he was destroying, the Lord beheld, and he repented him of the evil, and said to the angel that destroyed, It is enough, stay now thine hand. And the angel of the Lord stood by the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite. 16- And David lifted up his eyes, and saw the angel of the Lord stand between the earth and the heaven, having a drawn sword in his hand stretched out over Jerusalem. Then David and the elders of Israel, who were clothed in sackcloth, fell upon their faces. 17- And David said unto God, Is it not I that commanded the people to be numbered? even I it is that have sinned and done evil indeed; but as for these sheep, what have they done? let thine hand, I pray thee, O Lord my God, be on me, and on my father's house; but not on thy people, that they should be plagued. 18- Then the angel of the Lord commanded Gad to say to David, that David should go up, and set up an altar unto the Lord in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite. 19- And David went up at the saying of Gad, which he spake in the name of the Lord. 20- And Ornan turned back, and saw the angel; and his four sons with him hid themselves. Now Ornan was threshing wheat. 21- And as David came to Ornan, Ornan looked and saw David, and went out of the threshingfloor, and bowed himself to David with his face to the ground. 22- Then David said to Ornan, Grant me the place of this threshingfloor, that I may build an altar therein unto the Lord: thou shalt grant it me for the full price: that the plague may be stayed from the people.

23- And Ornan said unto David, Take it to thee, and let my lord the king do that which is good in his eyes: lo, I give thee the oxen also for burnt offerings, and the threshing instruments for wood, and the wheat for the meat offering; I give it all. 24- And king David said to Ornan, Nay; but I will verily buy it for the full price: for I will not take that which is thine for the Lord, nor offer burnt offerings without cost. 25- So David gave to Ornan for the place six hundred shekels of gold by weight. 26- And David built there an altar unto the Lord, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and called upon the Lord; and he answered him from heaven by fire upon the altar of burnt offering. 27- And the Lord commanded the angel; and he put up his sword again into the sheath thereof. 28- At that time when David saw that the Lord had answered him in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite, then he sacrificed there.

29- For the tabernacle of the Lord, which Moses made in the wilderness, and the altar of the burnt offering, were at that season in the high place at Gibeon. 30- But David could not go before it to enquire of God: for he was afraid because of the sword of the angel of the Lord.

After David saw with his own eyes the fire come down from heaven and accept his burnt offerings and sacrifices, he felt that this was the place God had chosen for the building of His Temple, so he set about with all diligence and joy to prepare the building materials for this Temple, to help his son Solomon, because he was young in age and the Temple would be great, to befit the greatness of God. It may seem strange that God chose the threshing floor of a Gentile man, Ornan the Jebusite, on which to build His Temple, but God declares here in the Old Testament that He will die to redeem the Jews and the Gentiles, and that His Church will be of all the peoples who believe in Him.

The place where the Temple was built was a threshing floor, that is, a place for gathering wheat and separating the grain from the chaff, and this is what will happen in the Church of the New Testament, of which John the Baptist spoke clearly in his Gospel (Mt 3:12).
The strangers: the Canaanites who live among the children of Israel.

David employed the pagan Canaanites in the heavy labor, which was hewing the stones with which the Temple would be built, and he put them to this work. The participation of the Gentiles in the building of the Temple is a type of their acceptance into the Church of the New Testament with the Jews.

Solomon also employed these strangers in the work of building the Temple, and their number is mentioned, which is 153,600 (2 Chr 2:17). Thus we see the sharing of David and Solomon in the building of the Temple, and both are types of Christ: David is a type of Christ's humility and endurance, and Solomon is a type of Christ's power and authority.
Doors: the leaves of the doors.

Joinings: the metal parts that join the doors to their jambs, which are called hinges. David also prepared large quantities of iron and brass; gifts had come to him from the surrounding nations, in addition to the spoil he took from the lands he conquered. Although brass was scarce in those times, David prepared a very great amount of it, which he could not count because of its abundance.

The Zidonians: the inhabitants of Zidon, a coastal city lying on the Mediterranean Sea north of the land of the Jews (present-day Lebanon), famous for fishing and for skill in cutting timber. The Tyrians: the inhabitants of Tyre, a coastal city lying on the Mediterranean Sea, north of the land of the Jews (present-day Lebanon) and south of Zidon; it was one of the greatest commercial cities in the world, and was famous for skill in cutting timber.
David also prepared large quantities of precious cedar wood, which reached him from the Tyrians and the Zidonians.
Tender: the small plant before it ripens, and what is meant here is that he is young, his character and strength not yet complete.
David's concern in preparing for the house of God had two reasons behind it:
1- His love for God, which made him concerned to prepare for His house, and he was not troubled, because of his humility, that God had forbidden him to build the house.
2- His love for his son Solomon, who felt the difficulty of the responsibility upon him because of his young age, for he began his reign when he was twenty years old.

May you be concerned to help those around you, especially in spiritual works and service, even if your name does not appear in this work. Be humble, and it is enough blessing for you that you shared in the service of God.

The most important thing David charged his son with was the building of the house of God, and he called God the God of Israel, because they were the only people at that time who worshiped God in the midst of the pagan nations, and therefore they are responsible for magnifying His name and worshiping Him, that perhaps the nations may understand and believe in Him.
David made clear to Solomon his desire to build the house of God, and that he had told God of this desire of his.

God refused David's desire to build a house for Him, because of his involvement in many wars with the surrounding nations, during which he killed many of them, or perhaps because of his killing of Uriah the husband of Bathsheba. God wanted the one who builds His house to be marked by calm and peace, because His house is a place of rest and peace for hearts. God promised David that He would give him a son whom he would name Solomon, whose days would be characterized by calm, as the peoples would be subject to him, so that he would be free for this great work, which was the building of the house of God.
God also promised to care for Solomon, so that he would be called a son to God and his kingdom would be established forever, because from his descendants Christ would come, who reigns forever.

Solomon here is a type of Christ, the only Son of the Father, who reigns forever. And thus we see that God worked through David to subdue the peoples who opposed His people. He also works through Solomon to build His house, for God is the worker in both, so that no one may be proud, just as He worked through Moses to bring the people out of Egypt, cross the wilderness, receive the commandments and build the tabernacle of meeting, while the possession of the land of Canaan was by the hand of Joshua.
Prosper: succeed.

After David had told his son Solomon the commands of God, he encouraged him to prepare for the building of the Temple, confident that God would make him succeed. Here we remember God's encouragement to Joshua, that he should arise and possess the land of Canaan (Josh 1:7, 8).
Statutes: worship.
Judgments: the commandments and the Law.
Understanding: wisdom and intelligence.

David charged Solomon to hold fast to the Law of God and His worship, for this is the foundation by which God is pleased, so that He will be with him, and then he will be able to build a temple for God, and God will give him wisdom and understanding to construct this great house. Solomon's responsibility is not only to hold fast to the statutes and judgments, but to lead his people to hold fast to them, and then he will be a king from God, to accomplish His purposes.
In the end David encouraged Solomon to carry out his responsibilities and not to fear any problems that might stand in his way, because God is his supporter and the One who works in him.

To encourage Solomon, David told him about the period of his reign, in which he suffered the troubles of the surrounding nations and problems within his kingdom, such as the rising up of his son Absalom against him. During this suffering, David's heart was occupied with the building of the house of God, so he prepared:
1- The building materials, in abundance beyond human expectations, which are:
a- 100,000 talents of gold
b- A million talents of silver
c- Brass and iron without number
d- Timber and stone without number
2- He also prepared craftsmen skilled in all the fields that the Temple needs, such as stonecutters, builders, carpenters ....
In the end David called Solomon to arise and build the house of God.

To succeed in any work, you must rely on God by obeying His commandments and holding fast to His worship, that is, your prayers, your fasts and all that you learn from the Church, in addition to constant repentance, that you may remain pure and a vessel fit for the work of God.

entries.section: (3) David's charge to the leaders of the people

paragraphs.text: David gathered the leaders of the people and reminded them how God had given them rest and peace, by subduing to them all the surrounding peoples by the hand of David.

entries.section: (3) David's charge to the leaders of the people

paragraphs.text: David charged the leaders to be concerned to love God with all their hearts, for it is the most important thing in life, and then they would be able to come forward to build His Temple, and place in it the ark of His covenant and the holy vessels. By this David supported his son Solomon, as he made the leaders of the people supporters of him in building this great Temple.

To be able to succeed in any work, your heart must be with God, and as you love Him you trust in Him, and go forward with confidence and strength and succeed in everything your hands reach for, and do not fear any troubles that may meet you. The service of the Levites. Chapters 23-26 speak of the service of the Levites for the Temple of God, and each chapter speaks of one of their classes, and this chapter speaks of the service of the Levites in general.

Solomon was not David's firstborn, but God chose him by name to be David's successor on his throne. So when David was old, that is, at the end of his sixties (for he died at the age of seventy), he made Solomon king in Jerusalem, so that his brothers would not oppose him, as Adonijah tried to seize the kingship.

David gathered the leaders of the people and also all the priests and the Levites, and by this he established Solomon's kingship, and he involved the leaders in the preparation for the service of the Temple. Then he commanded that the Levites be numbered from thirty years old and upward, and their number was 38,000, which is about four times their number in the days of Moses, when it was 8,580 (Num 4:47, 48). Here we see David's concern for arranging the service of the Temple and not only its building, for the service that is carried out in it is more important than its building, and all this shows David's great love for God, who until the end of his life, despite his old age, was concerned for the service of God.

Because David's numbering of the Levites was on account of preparing them for the service of the Temple, God did not punish him, as He punished him when he numbered the men of war, for the aim was the love of God and not pride.
If the love of God reigns over your heart, you will be concerned for His service, and indeed you will continue in this throughout your life, because through it you touch God and enjoy His blessings.
Officers: chiefs, or officers.
David divided the Levites into groups as follows:
1- He appointed 24 divisions, each of 1000 men, to help in the service of the Temple. Each division served for a week, that is, each division served twice every year.
2- He also appointed six thousand of the Levites as officers and judges, to decide disputes among the people.
3- He also assigned four thousand to guard the Temple, or as doorkeepers; the details of their service are mentioned in (ch. 9, ch. 26).
4- And he appointed another four thousand to praise with musical instruments.
Note:

The legal age for service is thirty years, but sometimes Levites of 25 or 20 years and above were added to the service, according to need, and they would help the Levites who were thirty years old and above (Num 4:3, Num 8:24).
Aaron had four sons, two of whom died because they offered strange fire (Num 3:4), and two remained, Eleazar and Ithamar.

David met with Zadok the high priest, who was of the descendants of Eleazar, and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar the other high priest, that is, the king met with the chiefs of the priests to divide the priests into divisions. Here we see the importance of organization in service and of defining responsibility, so that the work may be accomplished with success, order and arrangement.
Note: Abiathar the high priest was the father of Ahimelech, and his father was also called Ahimelech (1 Sam 23:6).

May you divide your responsibilities, to carry out each one at its proper time every day, or every week, or more, so that your responsibilities are accomplished with success and precision, and so that you do not forget any responsibility, and God will rejoice in your organization and your care.

Eleazar had 16 chiefs among his descendants, while Abiathar had fewer descendants, eight chiefs, and so the divisions of the priests were divided into 24 divisions. We notice that the Book of Revelation speaks to us of 24 priests (Rev 4:4), like the number of the twenty-four divisions of the priests mentioned here. The fewer descendants of Abiathar the high priest were due to God's curse on the house of Eli and his descendants, so their number became small (1 Sam 2:30, 31).

Lots were cast among the twenty-four chiefs to arrange them in the service of the sanctuary and the house of God. Perhaps the sanctuary means the ark of the covenant that was in Jerusalem, while the house of God is the tabernacle that was in Gibeon. After the building of the Temple, these divisions worked in its service and in all that it contained. Perhaps the division and the election by lot was to know who would begin the service, and then who would follow, since each division served for a week and then rested, and in the second half of the year served another week in order, with all the divisions meeting together at the great feasts.

The lot is a system that guarantees justice, with no partiality toward anyone (Prov 16:33), so that each one is assured his opportunity before God, as happened with the Apostles when they chose a replacement for Judas Iscariot (Acts 1:26).

The lots were cast, and perhaps this was by writing the names of the sons of Eleazar, each on a piece of pottery, and putting them in one jar, and the sons of Ithamar in another jar, and then they would take one from this jar and one from the other jar, while Shemaiah the scribe, one of the Levites, wrote the names of the divisions in order as it appeared from the lot. So after he wrote eight of the descendants of Eleazar and the eight who were of the descendants of Ithamar, he wrote the remaining eight of the descendants of Eleazar. All of this was by lot.
He mentions the names that came out by lot, that is, the order of the twenty-four divisions, so that they might begin their priestly service.

Our teacher St. Luke the Evangelist tells us that Zacharias the priest, the father of John the Baptist, was of the division of Abijah, that is, the eighth division (Lk 1:5). The twenty-four divisions of the priests continued as a system in force until the days of Christ, as shown by the mention that Zacharias was of the division of Abijah, and that his turn of service came, so he entered the Temple and saw the angel in the sanctuary.

entries.section: (1) The sons of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun

paragraphs.text: The captains of the host: what is meant is the host of God that serves Him, that is, the chief priests, and perhaps they are the chiefs of the twenty-four priestly divisions (ch. 24:7-19). Three men were distinguished in praise and singing, for their voices and their ability to play musical instruments, namely Asaph of the clan of the Gershonites, Heman of the clan of the Kohathites, and Jeduthun, who is also called Ethan (ch. 6:44), of the sons of Merari; that is, the chiefs of the singers were from all the clans of the Levites. David set them apart for the service of praise and prophesying, that is, chanting the psalms that are full of prophecies, for praise may be called prophesying, as it was in the days of Samuel (1 Sam 10:5). The musical instruments used were psalteries, harps and cymbals.
The service of praise and singing before the house of the Lord was a great work, because it is a spiritual work, full of feeling and of the repetition of the word of God, which satisfies the soul.
The sons of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun were organized into divisions to carry out the service of praise before the house of God continually.

entries.section: (1) The sons of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun

paragraphs.text: Here he mentions the sons of Asaph, who are four, and the sons of Jeduthun, who are six, although the sixth, who is Shimei, is not mentioned here but is mentioned in (v. 17). And the sons of Heman are fourteen. All these praised and gave thanks to God by the side of the king, that is, before the house of the Lord.

He singles out Heman as "the seer," and what is meant is that he sees the word of God that is in the psalms and declares it before the king, and perhaps he had a standing and spirituality that made the Bible give him the title of seer. Heman's praise was great in the eyes of God, so his singing was described as "to lift up the horn," and the horn is the horn of an animal, which is a symbol of strength, and the horn was also used as a musical instrument like the trumpet. Among God's blessings on Heman was that He gave him 14 sons and three daughters whom he taught the praise of God, and they excelled in it and led others in praise.
Here we see the fathers' concern to teach praise, so they loved it and it became their service, in which they were distinguished before God.

Be concerned to teach your children how to love God, especially through the ways that you love, such as the Liturgies, or the Midnight Praise (Tasbeha), or the Agpeya, or the Bible ... for what you love you will speak of from your heart and it will reach the hearts of your children, whether in the home, or in the Church, or among all whom you love and who love you, and so you will rejoice the heart of God, and your spiritual depth will increase, and you will be established in the service of God.

entries.section: (1) The sons of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun

paragraphs.text: The number of singers from the descendants of Asaph, Jeduthun and Heman was 288 men. The service of praise was under the leadership of the three chiefs mentioned, and these singers acquired an experience in praise that drew the hearts of the worshipers who came to the house of God.

The writer of this book pointed out in (ch. 23:1) that David had grown old and made his son Solomon king, and after this in (chs. 23 - 27) he mentioned the arrangements that David had prepared for the building of the Temple and the order of service in it. David had grown very old, as is mentioned in (1 Kgs 1:1, 2), so that he could not bear the cold of the air, and they covered him with clothes and he needed a nurse. But he strengthened himself to bid farewell to his people and charge them how to walk with God, and to declare Solomon king after him. So he gathered all his princes, that is, all those in authority in his kingdom, among them the captains of the divisions that served him, a division each month, mentioned in (ch. 24), and he mentions among them the eunuchs. This is the first time we find mention of this class with the kings of the people of God, although it existed with the kings of the nations. This means either that the people of God imitated the nations and castrated some people to serve the women, or that it was a rank in which this name, eunuchs, was used, but they were ordinary people.
David was eager and strengthened himself, so he rose from his bed and stood on his feet, that is, he did not sit on a throne and speak as kings customarily do, and this shows:
1- David's humility and his love for his people, which he confirms by his saying "my brethren, and my people."
2- David's concern to charge his people to submit to God.
3- His concern to declare Solomon's kingship.

4- His longing to build a house in which the ark of the covenant of God would rest (a resting place), to be a footstool for the feet of God, since His throne is in heaven, because the ark used to be moved about before this, when it was in the tabernacle of meeting.
5- David's sense that this was the last word he would address to his people made him revive.
In humility David declares his unworthiness to build the house of the Lord, as God declared to him, because he was occupied throughout his life with many wars.

David's submission is shown in his thanking God for choosing him as king, because God chose the tribe of Judah and from it the house of Jesse, from which God chose David. Although Judah was not the firstborn of Jacob, nor was David the firstborn of Jesse, it was the grace of God that gave him to become king. So he declares his unworthiness of the kingship and affirms that God is the One who chose him, and then afterward chose his son Solomon by name to reign after him, so that no one would object to him.

David declared clearly that God had chosen Solomon and also charged him with building His house, and he declared God's fatherhood and care for Solomon, and His readiness to establish his kingdom forever, on condition that Solomon submit to the commandments of God. This was a type of what actually happened, for Christ came from the descendants of David and Solomon to reign forever.

David concludes his word to the leaders of his people with the necessity of keeping the commandments of God and submitting to Him, so that the land of Canaan may remain an inheritance for them, and it is a symbol of the new earth, that is, the Kingdom of Heaven. This address, David declares, is in the sight of the Lord and in the audience of His congregation, that is, God is present and a witness to David's words, so that He may make His people submit and hold fast to the commandments of God.

Your way to happiness and to receiving all of God's blessings is to hold fast to His commandments, so read the word of God every day and examine yourself by it, if you have strayed from it, and God will establish you in His house and give you a place in His Kingdom.

entries.section: (2) David's charge to Solomon and his handing over to him the plan for building the house

paragraphs.text: After David charged his leaders, he gave a special charge to his son Solomon, because he would be the leader of the kingdom after him, and he commanded him as follows:

1- To know God, that is, to recall His works with the fathers and to know His commandments, and David here affirms to Solomon that He is "the God of thy father," because Solomon loves David, and this increases his holding fast to God.

2- To worship God with all that the Law and its rites prescribe, and that this be with all his heart and with longing and desire, that is, he should seek the worship of God in order to perform it enjoying it.

3- To remember that God knows hidden things, so that he is with Him with all his heart, and worship is not a mere outward performance, and he does not sin, because God sees him, even in his private room, away from eyes.

4- David encourages Solomon that if he holds fast to the commandments of God and His worship, he will feel God's presence with him and His blessing keeping and covering him, and he warns him that if he is negligent and leaves the commandments of God, God will forsake him and reject him because of his persistence in sin, and nothing awaits him but eternal torment.
5- He reminded him of the grace of God in choosing him to build the house of the Lord, and commanded him to be strong and work with all his heart.

Be concerned to charge your children and those around you and teach them the commandments of God, and even if they reject your words, they may act on them after a while. Do not be lazy because of your preoccupations, or because those around you do not listen, and your prayer for them will support them and encourage them to live with God.

entries.section: (2) David's charge to Solomon and his handing over to him the plan for building the house

paragraphs.text: Porch: the court. The upper chambers thereof: upper rooms. The inner chambers thereof: its rooms. The house of the mercy seat: the Holy of Holies, where the ark is covered by the cherubim.
Snuffers: those for the lampstands, to trim their lamps and light them.

Basons: for sprinkling water or blood. Cups: goblets. God declared to David the details of the building of the Temple precisely and in writing, and it may have been by means of an angel.
